title: Ask for review of a real estate assessment and appeal to the Board of Equalization
question: I think my Staunton real estate assessment is too high. How do I ask for a review and appeal it, and what are the deadlines?
summary: Staunton's City Assessor reassesses all real estate every two years, in odd-numbered years, at fair market value as of January 1. The next reassessment takes effect January 1, 2027, and notices usually go out at the end of January. A parcel whose value changes in another year, for example after new construction, also gets a notice, which states that year's deadlines. First ask the Assessor's Office for a review within 30 calendar days of the mailing. In the next 30 days the office takes written appeals to the Board of Equalization, on forms that come only from the office; only those who file by the deadline are heard. For the 2026 change notices the deadlines were 5 p.m. March 23 and 5 p.m. April 23, 2026. If the Board's decision does not satisfy you, you can apply to the Staunton Circuit Court. Keep paying the tax bill on time while you appeal. No fee was found for the review or the Board.

steps.step: Read the notice of assessment when it arrives
steps.who: City Assessor's Office (mails the notice); property owner
steps.how: Staunton reassesses all real estate every two years, in odd-numbered years, with values effective January 1. The next reassessment takes effect January 1, 2027, and those notices are usually mailed at the end of January. New construction and renovation are added every year, so an owner whose value changes in another year also gets a notice. State law says the notice must show the new value and the values for the two prior tax years, when and where you can object, and your right to see the Assessor's records. The notice also gives that year's appeal deadlines.
steps.deadline: Notices are typically mailed at the end of January of the new assessment year; state law requires mailing at least 15 days before the hearing on objections (Va. Code § 58.1-3330(A))
steps.quote: Following a change in assessment, a "Notice of Assessment" is sent to each property owner informing them of the new assessed value of their property and the deadlines for filing an appeal.

steps.step: Check the property record and ask for the assessment records
steps.who: Property owner or authorized representative; City Assessor's Office
steps.how: Check the facts the city holds for your parcel in the Real Estate Database linked from the City Assessor's page. After notices are mailed, state law opens the property appraisal cards to inspection and lets you examine the working papers behind your value. On request the Assessor must make available the method used, including the capitalization rate, the comparable properties or sales considered, and any other market surveys or factors, and must give a written explanation of an increase. The records are open during normal office hours; if the office sets a shorter inspection period, it cannot be less than four hours a day, Monday through Friday, on days the office is open. The city's Appeal Process page says the official assessment records are kept by the City Assessor's Office.
steps.quote: the assessing officer shall provide a written explanation or justification for an increase in the property's assessed value.

steps.step: If someone will act for you, file a letter of authorization with the Assessor
steps.who: Property owner (signs); agent; City Assessor's Office
steps.how: An agent, such as a consultant or tax company, can represent you in the Assessor's review and the Board appeal only with a letter of authorization filed with the City Assessor's Office. The city's page says the letter must be an original addressed to the Office of the City Assessor; identify the owner of record, the owner's address and phone number, the parcel ID number and the property address; name the agent company with its address and phone number; state the specific tax years (current and past years only; an open-ended authorization is not accepted); and carry the notarized signature of the owner of record or, for a corporation, of an officer authorized to act for it, with the printed or typed name and title. Authorizations must be renewed every year. The same letter covers both the Assessor's review and the Board appeal, but an agent needs a separate, specific authorization to sign income and expense forms. State law presumes a properly notarized letter from the owner to be a valid designation of a representative before the Board.
steps.deadline: No deadline stated; the letter names specific tax years and must be renewed yearly
steps.quote: Property owners who wish to be represented by an agent in matters concerning the assessment of real estate must provide a letter of authorization to the Office of the City Assessor.

steps.step: Ask the City Assessor's Office to review the assessment (informal appeal)
steps.who: Property owner or authorized representative; City Assessor's Office appraisers
steps.how: Call the office at 540.332.3827 (Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.), visit it on the first floor of City Hall (116 W. Beverley St.), or email its assessment appeals mailbox. The city's Appeal Process page highly encourages appointments, so that the right appraiser is available. Explain why you think the value is wrong. The FAQ says the basis for an appeal must include one or both of two reasons: the property is not assessed at its fair market value, or it is not assessed equitably with other similar properties; the Appeal Process page also lists incorrect factual information about the property. Bring evidence such as recent sales of similar properties, an appraisal, or photos of condition. Staff review the property information with you, explain how the value was reached, and may schedule an inspection; you also have the right to ask the Assessor to make a physical inspection. The Appeal Process page says appeal forms may be picked up in person, or mailed or emailed to the owner or authorized representative. An agent needs a letter of authorization on file (see the previous step).
steps.deadline: 30 calendar days from the date the notices were mailed, by 5 p.m. on the date the notice gives (for the 2026 change notices: 5 p.m., March 23, 2026)
steps.quote: The Assessor's Office accepts informal appeals for 30 calendar days from the date of the mailing.

steps.step: Prepare evidence for the Board of Equalization
steps.how: Before the Board, the Assessor's value is presumed correct. You carry the burden to show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the property is valued above fair market value or is not assessed uniformly, and that the value was not reached by generally accepted appraisal practice. Mistakes of fact that affect the assessment, including computation errors such as a wrong square footage or a math error, count as not following accepted practice. The Assessor values property by comparing sales, by cost and, mainly for commercial property, by income, so evidence of those kinds is the most useful. The Board may consider income and expense statements and market sales through the December 31 before the assessment's effective date, as long as they reach it by the city's deadline for applying to the Board. Studies or analyses published after that December 31 cannot be considered.
steps.deadline: Give income, expense and sales evidence to the Board by the city's deadline for applying to it; Va. Code § 58.1-3379(C) protects its consideration only if it is submitted by then
steps.quote: In all cases brought before the board, there shall be a presumption that the valuation determined by the assessor is correct.

steps.step: File a written appeal to the Board of Equalization with the City Assessor's Office
steps.who: Property owner, lessee or authorized representative; City Assessor's Office (accepts appeals on the Board's behalf)
steps.how: If the review does not settle it, file a formal written appeal to the Board of Equalization. The Assessor's Office takes these appeals for the Board during a second 30-day period that follows the review period. Board appeal forms must be obtained from the Assessor's Office: ask by phone (540.332.3827), by email to the assessment appeals mailbox, or in person; no copy is posted online. For residential property, state law says a hearing cannot be denied for lack of information if the application gives the address, the parcel number and the value you think is right. For commercial, multifamily residential or industrial property, the same protection also requires documentation of any assessment methodologies you rely on to be submitted with the application. A paper application sent by mail counts as received on its postmark date. An agent needs a letter of authorization on file; the same letter covers the Assessor's review and the Board appeal.
steps.deadline: During the 30-day period that follows the Assessor's 30-day review period, by 5 p.m. on the date the notice gives (for the 2026 change notices: 5 p.m., April 23, 2026). State law: the date may be set by ordinance and may not be earlier than 30 days after the Assessor's period for objections ends (Va. Code § 58.1-3378)
steps.quote: the Assessor's Office accepts formal written appeals on behalf of the Board of Equalization.

steps.step: Attend the Board of Equalization hearing
steps.who: Board of Equalization (appointed by the Staunton Circuit Court); City Assessor's Office; property owner
steps.how: The Board meets as soon as practicable after the filing period ends, and notice of each sitting is published in a newspaper at least seven days ahead. The city's notice says only those who filed Board appeal forms with the City Assessor before the deadline will be heard, no walk-ins are accepted, and the Board meets in the Caucus Room of City Hall, 116 W. Beverley Street, in a meeting open to the public. For residential property with fewer than four units, the Assessor must send you a written notice at least 45 days before your hearing that explains your right to copies of the assessment records and to ask for a physical inspection; if you ask in writing, the records must be provided within 15 days. The city describes the Board as three local property owners, including a licensed appraiser, a realtor and an attorney. The Board may inspect the property. It can lower, raise or keep the value, and it has a duty to raise assessments as well as lower them where needed to equalize them, but it cannot raise yours until you have been notified and given a chance to show cause against the increase. For commercial, multifamily residential or industrial property, the Board cannot raise the value unless the Assessor recommends it, and if the Assessor asks the Board to raise it after you appeal, the Assessor must tell you at least 14 days before the hearing.
steps.deadline: As soon as practicable after the second 30-day period ends (the 2026 notice gave the time and date as to be determined); for residential property with fewer than four units, the Assessor's written notice comes at least 45 days before the hearing (Va. Code § 58.1-3331(E))
steps.quote: Only those persons who filed Board appeal forms with the City Assessor prior to the deadline will be heard.

steps.who: Board of Equalization; Commissioner of the Revenue (receives copies of orders); City Treasurer (bills and refunds)
steps.how: The Board decides each appeal by order and promptly sends a copy of any order that raises or lowers an assessment to you and to the Commissioner of the Revenue. If the order lowers the value after you have paid, ask the City Treasurer how the difference will be refunded. City Code Chapter 3.55 covers refunds of taxes paid in error and interest on erroneous assessments; only its headings have been checked.
steps.quote: transmit promptly copies of such orders as relate to the increase or decrease of assessments to the taxpayer and commissioner of the revenue.

steps.step: If you still disagree, apply to the Staunton Circuit Court
steps.who: Property owner (often with a lawyer); Staunton Circuit Court; City Attorney (defends the city)
steps.how: File an application to correct the assessment with the Clerk of the Staunton Circuit Court, 113 East Beverley Street (Clerk's Office on the third floor), naming the locality as "City of Staunton." The City Attorney defends the city, and a judge hears the case without a jury. The value set by the Assessor, or as changed by the Board, is presumed correct, and you must prove it wrong by a preponderance of the evidence. If the court finds the value above fair market value it may reduce it; if it finds the assessment erroneous and the tax has been paid, it must order the excess refunded with interest, unless the error came from your wilful failure or refusal to give the assessing office information the law requires. If it finds the value below fair market value it must raise it and order you to pay the proper tax. State law also lets an owner go to court without first going to the Board where the Board is not a prerequisite; the sources read do not say whether it is one in Staunton.
steps.deadline: Within three years from the last day of the tax year for which the assessment is made, within one year from the date of the assessment, or within one year from a final determination by the assessing official under § 58.1-3981, whichever is later (Va. Code § 58.1-3984(A)); an appeal from the Board's order has the same time limit (§ 58.1-3382)
steps.fee: Clerk's fee of $60 (civil action without a claim for money damages) plus the $8 Technology Trust Fund Fee; other court costs may apply (see fees)
steps.quote: If the property owner is not satisfied with the decision of the Board of Equalization, he or she may appeal further to the local Circuit Court.

steps.step: Keep paying the tax bill on time while the appeal is pending
steps.how: Bills based on the January 1 assessment are usually sent in early May. Seventy-five percent of the bill is due June 20 and the remaining 25% on December 5; where a mortgage company pays from escrow, the whole escrow amount is due June 20. State law says a tax bill is not delinquent or subject to collection while an administrative appeal under Va. Code § 58.1-3980 (an application to the Commissioner of the Revenue or other official for correction) is pending, if it was filed within 90 days of the date of the assessment, and for 30 days after the final decision; interest provided by law can still be charged afterwards on any part found owed. The pages read do not say whether the Assessor's review or a Board appeal counts as such an appeal, so pay on time to avoid penalty and interest. At the current rate of $0.91 per $100 of assessed value, each $10,000 of assessed value is $91 a year in tax.
steps.deadline: June 20 (75% of the bill) and December 5 (the remaining 25%)
steps.quote: Seventy-five percent of the tax bill is due on June 20th, with the remaining 25% due on the following December 5th.

caveats: The City of Staunton's website (www.ci.staunton.va.us) refuses automated readers, so the city pages and PDFs cited here are Internet Archive copies: they show the pages as they were when copied. The Real Estate Tax FAQs' appeal section is the same in its copies of 2026-06-15 and 2026-02-10. The live pages may have changed since; confirm on them or by phone before you act.

The Appeal Process page (Internet Archive copy of 2026-06-15) says 2026 was an off year, with change notices to 394 properties; reviews by the Assessor were accepted until 5 p.m., March 23, 2026 and Board appeals until 5 p.m., April 23, 2026; requests could be made by phone, in person or by email to the assessment appeals mailbox; appointments are highly encouraged; Board appeal forms come only from the Assessor's Office; and only those who filed them before the deadline are heard, with no walk-ins. The page also lists incorrect factual information as a basis for appeal and says the Board meets in the City Hall Caucus Room in a public meeting. Form f2's URL and requirements are on the Letter of Authorization page.

Timing now. On 2026-10-11 the 2026 windows for the Assessor and the Board have closed. The next ones open with the notices for the January 1, 2027 reassessment, usually mailed at the end of January 2027. For a 2026 assessment the circuit court route stays open: assuming the tax year is the calendar year, three years from its last day runs to December 31, 2029 (Va. Code § 58.1-3984(A)).

Deadline source. State law lets City Council set the Board deadline by ordinance (Va. Code § 58.1-3378). In the City Code, only the tables of contents of the Charter, Title 2 (Administration) and Title 3 (Revenue and Finance) have been checked. None of their headings names the Assessor, the Board of Equalization or an appeal deadline. The two 30-day periods are taken from the city's FAQ, and the 2026 dates and 5 p.m. cutoffs from the Appeal Process page. Whether they are set by ordinance, by resolution or by office practice was not found. The 2027 dates were not yet published on the pages cited here.

Local ordinance not quoted. Staunton's code is on General Code's eCode360. Its terms limit content to personal use and forbid reproducing it for public purposes, so only headings were read. City Code §§ 3.55.010 and 3.55.020 are recorded by heading alone, and § 3.10.040 (by its heading, penalty and interest on late taxes) was not read.

Which Board. The FAQ describes a board of three local property owners, including a licensed appraiser, a realtor and an attorney. State law has the circuit court appoint a city's board in the tax year after a reassessment (Va. Code § 58.1-3370(A)), with a term ending one year after that assessment's effective date (§ 58.1-3370(B)). A city using the biennial method may instead have a permanent board (§ 58.1-3373). The Appeal Process page says the city conducts a general reassessment every two years, which points to § 58.1-3250 rather than the biennial assessment method of § 58.1-3253(A), yet its 2026 page still took Board appeals in an off year, and its Board notice speaks of equalizing the 2025 assessments. Whether Staunton has a permanent board is not settled here. The Board's page on the city's Granicus boards site refuses automated readers, so it is not described here.

The Assessor's review. The pages read do not say how the Assessor answers a review (for example by letter) or how long it takes. The relief in Va. Code §§ 58.1-3370(B) and 58.1-3378, when a decision comes after the Board's deadline, speaks of an application to 'the commissioner of the revenue or other official performing the duties imposed on commissioners of the revenue'. The correction route in §§ 58.1-3980 and 58.1-3981 is similar. Whether the City Assessor counts as that official, and whether an informal review counts as such an application, was not settled. File with the Board by its deadline rather than rely on these.

Board form and filing. No Board appeal form is posted online; the Appeal Process page says the forms must be obtained from the Assessor's Office, by phone, email or in person, so f1 points to that page. The pages read do not say whether a completed appeal can be returned by email. State law allows electronic filing only if the governing body provides for it, and always keeps the right to file on paper (Va. Code § 58.1-3378). The Appeal Process page's sentence that appeal forms may be picked up, mailed or emailed sits under the Assessor-review heading, so the review may also use a form; this was not settled.

Fees. No fee for the Assessor's review or for the Board was found in state law or on the city pages read. The $60 circuit court fee assumes the clerk files a tax assessment application as a civil action without a claim for money damages. Service of process and the local courthouse and law library assessments (Va. Code §§ 17.1-281, 42.1-70) depend on local choices that were not checked. Ask the Clerk's Office for the current costs.

Paying during an appeal. Va. Code §§ 58.1-3916 and 58.1-3958 keep a bill from being delinquent or subject to collection while an administrative appeal under § 58.1-3980 is pending, if it was filed within 90 days of the date of the assessment, and for 30 days after the final decision. Whether Staunton's Assessor review or a Board appeal is such an appeal was not determined, so this page advises paying the June 20 and December 5 amounts on time. If the value is lowered after payment, the court route orders a refund with interest (§ 58.1-3987). Refunds after an Assessor or Board change fall under City Code Chapter 3.55, which has not been checked.

Burden in court. Va. Code § 58.1-3984(B) presumes that the Assessor's value, or the Board's, is correct. It puts the burden on the owner to show by a preponderance of the evidence that the value is above (or below) fair market value or not uniform, and that it was not reached by generally accepted appraisal practice. If the court finds the value below fair market value it must raise it and order the proper tax paid (§ 58.1-3987). This is legal information, not advice; consider a lawyer or appraiser for a court case.

Augusta County. Staunton is an independent city surrounded by Augusta County. A property with a Staunton mailing address may lie in the county, which runs its own assessments and appeals. Check that the parcel is inside city limits.

Privacy. The City Assessor's page and FAQ give the Assessor's name and personal mailbox, and the Circuit Court page names the Clerk and the judges. Those are left out. Only office addresses, office phone lines and the role-shaped appeals mailbox are recorded.

State law. Code of Virginia quotes are from Open US Law's copy of the cited section; that copy's spacing before punctuation after cross-references (for example '§ 58.1-3330 .') is kept. The law.lis.virginia.gov URLs are for reference. Va. Code § 58.1-3381(B), which keeps a Board value presumptively correct for two more years, says it applies to the City of Virginia Beach and is not used here.
